newsitem.title: UK: Dollar firm in European ahead of U.S. CPI data.
newsitem.headline: Dollar firm in European ahead of U.S. CPI data.

text.p: The dollar was firm at midday Europe, just off session highs against the mark ahead of U.S. February consumer price data, the last batch of inflationary data before next week's Federal Open Market Committee meeting.
Market speculation of a rate rise at the March 25 meeting has been simmering for some time and is partly responsible for the dollar's underlying strength.
However, currency analysts were still wary of the importance of the CPI data in providing clues to likely monetary policy action the Federal Reserve will take.

"It is an important figure with the market on a knife-edge in the run-up to the FOMC, but you could say it's the wrong figure at the right time," said Francis Breedon, foreign exchange economist at Lehman Brothers in London.
Analysts were mindful that Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has indicated that other factors, such as labour market conditions, were more determinant to Fed monetary policy.
Nevertheless, today's data will be watched closely and even a slight deviation from forecasts could trigger a sharp market reaction.
An average of analysts' forecasts point to a 0.2 percent rise in February CPI against January's 0.1 percent rise. Year-on-year, the headline figure is expected to show 3.1 percent growth.
At midday trade in Europe, the dollar against the German mark was trading at 1.6841, just shy of its session highs and well-above its late Tuesday level of 1.6731 marks.
On the yen, the dollar was also firm and stood at 123.14 against 122.48 on Tuesday.

"If we see an upturn in the CPI, it will harden the expectations that the Fed will raise rates next week," said Jeremy Stretch, currency strategist at NatWest Markets in London. "Tuesday's strong housing starts data has helped underpin that view."
Analysts said that, so far, there were few indications of any significant inflationary pressures in the U.S. and labour costs remained subdued.
But currency markets were wary of the risk of a pre-emptive strike by the Fed to curb the risk of potential inflation.

"The basic problem is the market's fear of a pre-emptive move by the Fed which means the market can't relax," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN-Amro in London. "We have to see data biased in a softening direction to ease the sense of a Fed policy move."

The long-running positive growth, low inflation scenario being played out in the U.S. is also increasing nervousness for those convinced such a situation has to end at some point. And a rate hike next week would go a long way to alleviate those concerns and bolster credibility with the Fed, said analysts.

A strong CPI number today, and the attendant higher rate expectations, could spark a sell-off in U.S. assets. If this is large enough, it could prove to be a drag on the dollar as portolio flows shift out of U.S. assets, especially if followed by a rate rise next week.
"But in the end it has to be good for the dollar. A drop in assets, putting 30-year bond yields above 7.00 percent has to be positive for the dollar," said ABN-Amro's Norfield.

On the other hand, soft CPI data today may alleviate some of the higher rate speculation but the subsequent dollar retreat is also seen limited. Steady rates next week will also keep rate hike sentiment on the boil, maintaining one of the dollar's key props.

"Part of the dollar's strength is in expectations of higher U.S. rates," said NatWest's Stretch. "If a rate rise doesn't materialise, the economic situation is still positive in the U.S. and positive for the dollar."
